questions.question: In round $k$ of IESDS the reduced game has strategy sets $S_1^{k-1},\ldots,S_n^{k-1}$. Against which opponent profiles is a strategy of player $i$ checked for strict dominance?
options: All profiles $s_{-i}\in S_{-i}$ of the original game
Only the remaining profiles $s_{-i}\in S_{-i}^{k-1}$
Only the profiles deleted in earlier rounds
Only the opponent profile that player $i$ expects

questions.question: Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS) repeatedly deletes, in the current reduced game, every strategy that another remaining strategy of the same player beats against every remaining opponent profile. When is a finite game called dominance solvable?
options: When exactly one strategy profile survives the procedure
When at least one strategy is deleted in the first round
When every player has some strictly dominated strategy
When the procedure stops after a single round

questions.question: Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS) repeatedly deletes, in the current reduced game, every strategy that another remaining strategy of the same player beats against every remaining opponent profile. In a finite game, two students delete dominated strategies in different orders, one of them removing only one strategy per round. What can be said about their final results?
options: They may differ, as the order of deletion matters.
They agree only if both delete one strategy per round.
They reach the same set of surviving profiles.
The student who deletes more per round keeps fewer profiles.

questions.question: Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS) repeatedly deletes, in the current reduced game, every strategy that another remaining strategy of the same player beats against every remaining opponent profile. What must be assumed for a deletion in the first round to be justified?
options: That every player knows that this player is rational
Only that the player owning the deleted strategy is rational
That rationality is common knowledge among all players
That this player correctly predicts the others' choices

questions.question: Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS) repeatedly deletes, in the current reduced game, every strategy that another remaining strategy of the same player beats against every remaining opponent profile. In a finite game no player has a strictly dominated strategy in the original game. What does IESDS predict?
options: The profile with the highest total payoff.
Each player's strategy with the highest payoff.
No profile at all: the outcome is empty.
Nothing: every profile of the game survives.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses a row, player 2 a column; payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$: row $U$: $L$: $(2,1)$, $C$: $(0,3)$, $R$: $(3,0)$; row $D$: $L$: $(1,2)$, $C$: $(2,1)$, $R$: $(1,1)$. Which strategy is strictly dominated in round 1 of IESDS?
options: $R$, strictly dominated by $C$
$D$, strictly dominated by $U$
$R$, strictly dominated by $L$
$C$, strictly dominated by $L$

questions.question: A $2\times2$ game has payoff pairs $(v_1,v_2)$, with player 1 picking the row and player 2 the column: row $T$: $L$: $(3,1)$, $R$: $(2,0)$; row $B$: $L$: $(1,2)$, $R$: $(0,3)$. Apply iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies. Which profile remains?
options: All four profiles, as player 2 has no dominated strategy

questions.question: Player 1 chooses a row, player 2 a column; payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$: row $U$: $L$: $(3,2)$, $R$: $(0,1)$; row $M$: $L$: $(1,0)$, $R$: $(1,1)$; row $D$: $L$: $(2,0)$, $R$: $(-1,3)$. How many strategy profiles survive IESDS?

Player 1 chooses $U$, $M$ or $D$; player 2 chooses $L$ or $R$. Player 1's payoffs against $(L,R)$: $U$: $(3,0)$, $M$: $(0,3)$, $D$: $(1,1)$. In round 1, IESDS deletes $D$ only if one of the other pure strategies $U$, $M$ strictly dominates it. Is $D$ deleted?
options: Yes: $D$ is never player 1's best choice in any column.
Yes: $U$ and $M$ together beat $D$ in every column.
No: neither $U$ nor $M$ beats $D$ in both columns.
No: $D$ has the highest guaranteed payoff, so it is best.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $T$ or $B$; player 2 chooses $L$, $M$ or $R$; payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$: row $T$: $L$: $(4,2)$, $M$: $(3,3)$, $R$: $(1,0)$; row $B$: $L$: $(2,5)$, $M$: $(2,4)$, $R$: $(5,1)$. Round 1 deletes $R$. Why is $B$ deleted in round 2?
options: $T$ beats $B$ against both remaining columns: $4>2$, $3>2$.
$B$ is never player 1's best choice against column $L$.
$T$ beats $B$ against every column, $R$ included.
$B$ gives player 2 lower payoffs than $T$ does.

questions.question: Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS) repeatedly deletes, in the current reduced game, every strategy that another remaining strategy of the same player beats against every remaining opponent profile. A deletion happens in round $3$. Besides rationality, what does it require about knowledge of rationality?
options: One level: all know that everyone is rational
Three levels, one for each round so far
No levels: rationality alone is enough
Two levels of 'everyone knows that' about rationality

questions.question: Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS) repeatedly deletes, in the current reduced game, every strategy that another remaining strategy of the same player beats against every remaining opponent profile. Every player has a strictly dominant strategy, one that strictly beats each of his or her other strategies against every opponent profile. How does IESDS proceed?
options: It deletes nothing, since dominant strategies stop the procedure.
It needs one round per player, deleting one player at a time.
One round deletes every other strategy and leaves that profile.
It leaves every profile containing at least one dominant strategy.

questions.question: Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS) repeatedly deletes, in the current reduced game, every strategy that another remaining strategy of the same player beats against every remaining opponent profile. In a finite game, can IESDS delete all of some player's strategies?
options: Yes, when every strategy of the player is dominated by another.
Yes, when the opponent's strategies are deleted first.
No, because each round deletes one strategy only.
No: in each round some strategy of each player is undominated.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $T$ or $B$, player 2 chooses $L$ or $R$; payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$: $(T,L)=(2,1)$, $(T,R)=(0,0)$, $(B,L)=(0,0)$, $(B,R)=(1,2)$. IESDS deletes nothing here. Which single payoff change makes IESDS leave exactly one profile?
options: Raise $v_2(T,L)$ from $1$ to $3$
Raise $v_1(T,R)$ from $0$ to $2$
Lower $v_2(B,R)$ from $2$ to $0$
Raise $v_1(T,L)$ from $2$ to $5$

questions.question: Player 1's payoffs against player 2's $(L,R)$ are $T$: $(5,4)$, $M$: $(3,3)$, $B$: $(2,1)$. A student deletes $M$ first, as $T$ strictly dominates it. Can $B$, which $M$ also dominated, still be deleted?
options: No: $B$'s dominator $M$ has already been deleted.
Yes: $T$ strictly dominates $B$ too ($5>2$, $4>1$).
No: a second deletion must wait for player 2's round.
Yes, but only because $B$ was worse than $M$ before.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $T$ or $B$; player 2 chooses $L$, $M$ or $R$; payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$: row $T$: $L$: $(3,1)$, $M$: $(2,2)$, $R$: $(4,0)$; row $B$: $L$: $(1,2)$, $M$: $(1,1)$, $R$: $(0,0)$. Each round deletes every strictly dominated strategy of every player. How many rounds delete something, and what is the outcome?
options: Two rounds; $(T,M)$ is the outcome
Three rounds with one deletion each, reaching $(T,M)$
A single round removing $B$, $R$ and $L$ at once
Two rounds, but $R$ outlasts $M$ for player 2

questions.question: In a two-player game, strategy $B$ of player 1 is deleted in round 2 of IESDS, after player 2's strictly dominated strategy $R$ was deleted; against $R$, $B$ is player 1's best choice. Could a rational player 1 who doubts player 2's rationality choose $B$?
options: Yes: if he thinks $R$ likely, $B$ can be optimal for him.
No: a rational player never plays a deleted strategy.
No: $B$ is strictly dominated in the original game.
Yes, but only if player 1 is not rational.

questions.question: Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS) repeatedly deletes, in the current reduced game, every strategy that another remaining strategy of the same player beats against every remaining opponent profile. Why does deleting a strictly dominated strategy never remove a strategy that player $i$ could rationally use against some belief about the remaining opponent profiles?
options: Because a dominated strategy always gives player $i$ a negative payoff.
Because beliefs are ignored, so no strategy is ever optimal for a belief.
The dominator beats it against every remaining profile, so under every belief.
Because the dominating strategy is the unique best response to every profile.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $X$ or $Y$; player 2 chooses $a$, $b$ or $c$; payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$: row $X$: $a$: $(3,1)$, $b$: $(2,3)$, $c$: $(1,2)$; row $Y$: $a$: $(1,4)$, $b$: $(1,2)$, $c$: $(5,0)$. A student deletes only strategies dominated in the original game, then stops. What does he keep, and what does IESDS give?
options: He already ends at $(X,b)$, just like IESDS.
He keeps four profiles; IESDS ends at $(X,b)$.
He deletes nothing and keeps all six profiles.
He keeps four; IESDS removes $X$, ending at $(Y,a)$.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $T$, $M$ or $B$; player 2 chooses $L$, $C$ or $R$; payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$: row $T$: $L$: $(3,1)$, $C$: $(1,2)$, $R$: $(0,0)$; row $M$: $L$: $(2,0)$, $C$: $(2,3)$, $R$: $(1,1)$; row $B$: $L$: $(1,4)$, $C$: $(0,2)$, $R$: $(4,1)$. What is the IESDS outcome?
options: $\{T,M\}\times\{C\}$
$\{T,M,B\}\times\{L,C\}$
